🏆

How to Win a DECA Roleplay

Learn the parts of a roleplay, then watch a full Craft Path roleplay come together from the prep room to the handshake, then try one yourself.

Part 1 · The Parts of a Roleplay

What is a roleplay?

A roleplay is you acting out a business meeting. You get a scenario sheet with a problem, you prepare for 10 minutes, and then you present a solution to a judge who plays your boss or a client.

  1. 10 minutes of prep in a prep room, where you read the scenario and build your tents.
  2. 7 minutes with the judge. You present for about 5 minutes and the judge asks questions for the rest.
The goal: show the judge you understood the problem, have a real solution, and can explain your thinking. It should feel like a meeting, not a speech.

There are only four parts to understand: the scenario sheet, the performance indicators, the solution, and the tents. The next few pages cover each one. Then we'll walk through a full roleplay together.

Part 1 · The Parts of a Roleplay

The scenario sheet

Your scenario sheet has two sides. The front describes the situation. The back lists what a good solution looks like, the career competencies, and your performance indicators (PIs). This is the Craft Path sheet we'll use for the whole guide.

Front: event situation (Craft Path)
Back: solution, career competencies, and PIs

Find these three things first

  1. Your role: who you are playing. Here, a marketing communications specialist at Craft Path.
  2. The judge's role: who you are talking to. Here, the director of marketing. They're above you, so be professional.
  3. The situation: the actual problem to solve. Here, a strategy for National Selfie Day that gets younger people talking about Craft Path and posting selfies. This is the most important one. Everything you say should connect back to it.
You can assume things. If the sheet doesn't mention an app, a budget, or sponsored athletes, assume the company has them. Say it out loud ("I'm assuming we have an app") so it sounds confident. Just never assume something the sheet contradicts.
Part 1 · The Parts of a Roleplay

Performance indicators (PIs)

A PI is a concept you have to cover during the meeting. The judge scores each one separately. They aren't trick questions. They're literally telling you what to talk about.

Read the situation first. If you don't know the problem, the PIs won't make sense. Once you know it, each PI becomes a question you would have to answer anyway to solve the problem.

The Craft Path PIs

PI 1
Explain marketing and its importance in the global economy.
PI 2
Explain the nature of buzz marketing.
PI 3
Explain the use of video and images in digital marketing.
PI 4
Monitor user-generated content.
PI 5
Explain the nature of corporate branding.

How to cover a PI

Every PI gets the same three moves:

  1. Say what it is. You have to actually say the concept out loud. Define it in plain English.
  2. Say why it's important. Back it up with a reason, a stat, or a visual. This is usually where your drawing comes from.
  3. Say what we're doing with it. Connect it to this company and this problem by name.

Here's what that sounds like. This is not one of the Craft Path PIs. It's a made-up example using "Explain the nature of target markets," just to show the shape of a PI answer.

Example only · not a Craft Path PI

"As you know, target markets are groups you advertise to. what it is Now, we had to consider it because research shows it yields much greater results over the course of your campaign, as shown here. why it matters + visual So taking all of this into account, we determined our target market to be teen boys. what we're doing with it Now that we have our target market, we started focusing on what to market to them, so we had to consider different forms of marketing, like videos and images..." segue to next PI

Don't skip a PI. A great solution can't make up for a PI you left out. If you're short on time, shorten a PI, but never drop one.
Part 1 · The Parts of a Roleplay

The solution

The solution is scored on how unique, practical, and effective it is. Come up with it after you read the situation, before you write your tents, so every PI can build toward it.

Go-to solution types

  • Technology: an app, a platform, or a digital tool.
  • AI: automating tasks, analyzing data, or flagging content.
  • Social media: targeted posts, influencers, or campaigns.
  • Repurpose: take a tool the business already knows and point it at a new problem.

The best solutions combine a couple of these with a hook. The Craft Path solution we'll use: people take a photo in front of a Craft Path store and post it through the Craft Path app, which syncs to their socials. The state with the most posts gets ten people picked to meet one of Craft Path's sponsored athletes. Posting through the app lets Craft Path's AI flag posts it doesn't want to be affiliated with.

Be careful with the defaults. Tech, AI, and social media fit marketing and entrepreneurship events. In finance, hospitality, and HR, "we'd use AI" to fix an employee dispute sounds like a template. In those events, start with process (change the steps), training (change what people know), or cost structure (change where the money goes).
Part 1 · The Parts of a Roleplay

Tents

Tents are folded sheets of paper. They're your notes and your visuals at the same time, and they're where the whole roleplay comes to life.

  • One sheet per PI. Craft Path has 5 PIs, so 5 sheets.
  • Fold them all together in one stack so they stand up like tents.
  • Your side (faces you): the PI and your notes on it.
  • Judge's side (faces the judge): a drawing that explains something on that tent. A graph, a phone screen, stick figures. Anything.

When you present, you read off your side and point at the judge's side ("as you can see on the front here..."). Then you move to the next tent. You never shuffle papers.

Here's one of the real Craft Path tents. It opens on the judge's side. Click the button to flip it and see the notes side. Click any photo to zoom in.

Always draw something. A rough graph or a stick-figure sketch makes you look prepared. Judges see a lot of blank tents.
Judge's side (visual)

That's all four parts. Now let's walk through one together, start to finish, with the actual Craft Path tents.

Part 2 · Walkthrough · The 10-Minute Prep Room

Let's walk through one together: the prep room

You just sat down with the Craft Path sheet. Here's exactly what to do, in order.

Step 1: Pick up all 5 sheets and fold them together

One sheet per PI. Stack them and fold them in half all at once.

Step 2: Write one PI on each tent

Write the PI on your side of each tent, in order. Don't write answers yet.

Step 3: Read the situation and think of a solution

Find your role, the judge's role, and the problem. Then decide on your solution before you write anything else. For Craft Path: photos in front of a store, posted through the Craft Path app, state competition, meet a sponsored athlete.

Step 4: Pick the PI where you'll reveal the solution

Look at the PIs and find the one where the solution would make the most sense. In a marketing roleplay it's usually the PI about marketing materials. For Craft Path, that's PI 3, video and images, because the solution is people posting images. Everything before PI 3 sets up the plan. Everything after it defends the plan.

Step 5: Write the answer on each tent

For each PI, write what it is, why it's good to do, and what we're doing with it. Keep the notes short. Then draw the visual on the judge's side. Here are the real tents from this roleplay. Each one opens on the judge's side; flip it to see the notes.

Tent 1 · PI 1 · Marketing and the global economy
Marketing: doing things to get our name out there so more people buy our things. The global economy gets healthier through marketing (show the study on the front), which helps us, since a better global economy means more people buy our things.
Judge's side (visual)
Tent 2 · PI 2 · Buzz marketing
Posting about relevant things, like Adidas posting about the World Cup in June 2026. Important because more views (Adidas example on the front). Tie in this as a segue.
Judge's side (visual)
Tent 3 · PI 3 · Video and images · ★ REVEAL
Easy to spread, so they're more useful for marketing. Plan: people post a picture of themselves in front of a Craft Path on our app. Ten people are chosen to meet a sponsored athlete. The photos post to their socials too.
Judge's side (visual)
Tent 4 · PI 4 · Monitor user-generated content
Acknowledge people may post things we don't want to be related with. This is why we post on our app first, so our AI can flag potential posts to be taken down.
Judge's side (visual)
Tent 5 · PI 5 · Corporate branding
How people see us. Fun but professional, shown through selfies but also monitoring of photos. Conclusion: summarize the plan, affirm it's good, be open-minded to changes, transition into questions. The judge's side is just the list: Craft Path, fun, professional.
Judge's side (visual)
Notice how short the notes are. If you read these tents word for word, it would be a horrible roleplay. The notes are just what you need to cover. The presentation is where you turn them into a meeting, and that's the next page.
Part 2 · Walkthrough · The 7 Minutes With the Judge

The presentation: where it comes to life

This is the same Craft Path roleplay, spoken out loud, with the tent you're on beside each part. Read the script, then the note under each tent to see what that part is doing. Every PI is covered, every one connects to the situation, and the solution lands on PI 3.

Step 1: Shake their hand

Walk in, shake the judge's hand, say your name, and sit down. Then start the intro.

Step 2: The intro

Intro

"Thank you for meeting with me today. I saw your email about wanting to develop a marketing strategy for National Selfie Day, and the marketing team has been working very hard to make an amazing plan. But before I tell you the plan, I want to take you behind the scenes into what we had to consider when making this plan. And that was: what was the point of it anyway?"

What's happening: you repeat the problem in the judge's own words, promise a plan is coming, and that last question is a segue straight into PI 1.

Step 3: Set up the plan (PIs 1 and 2)

Tent 1 · PI 1 · Marketing and the global economy

"Well, the point of marketing is ultimately to do things to get our name out there so more people buy our things. And this is super important because it helps the global economy, which in turn helps us, since more people are willing to buy under a good economy, as detailed by these findings portrayed on the graphs in the front. So now that we knew why we had to do the marketing, we had to figure out what type of marketing."

Judge's side (visual)
What's happening: what it is, why it's important (pointing at the graphs), and the last sentence is the segue into PI 2.
Tent 2 · PI 2 · Buzz marketing

"And we landed on doing buzz marketing. As you know, buzz marketing is posting materials about some event that's relevant, which National Selfie Day is, around the time of relevancy. And we decided to use buzz marketing because it leads to more views, as shown in this post Adidas did during the World Cup. So we decided to post heavily around National Selfie Day to hype it up, and then put a lot of effort into it. Now that I have explained what we considered, I want to talk about the plan."

Judge's side (visual)
What's happening: "As you know" states the PI and boosts the judge's confidence. The Adidas post on the front is the example. Then a segue straight into the reveal.

Step 4: Reveal the plan (PI 3)

Tent 3 · PI 3 · Video and images · ★ the reveal

"The plan is we will use videos and images, since they spread faster on the internet. And we will specifically have people take photos in front of one of our stores and post it into our app, which will sync into their social medias. The state with the most posts will have ten members of that state meet with one of our most esteemed sponsored athletes. So that is the strategy that we came up with, and we think it will be good since it plays off of buzz marketing well, and the info will spread fast since they are images on socials as well."

Judge's side (visual)
What's happening: this one is special. It's no longer about setting up, it's about revealing. The PI (images spread fast) is the reason the plan works, and you tie it back to PI 2.

Step 5: Defend the plan (PIs 4 and 5)

Tent 4 · PI 4 · Monitor user-generated content

"Now, I realize that we may have some concerns about letting the public post anything they want to their Instagrams with us tagged in it. So to monitor their user posting in relation to how people view us, we will have them post on our app only. This will allow our AI to flag posts we don't want to be affiliated with, which is why we are only having them post on our platform."

Judge's side (visual)
What's happening: you raise the judge's concern before they do, name-drop the PI, and show how the plan handles it.
Tent 5 · PI 5 · Corporate branding

"Now, the main reason we are doing this is to protect our corporate image. As you know, corporate image is basically how people see us. And by doing this, we are affirming our corporate image of being fun and professional." [point to the list in the front]

Judge's side (visual)
What's happening: PI 5 skips the long "why it matters" and goes straight to how it applies to Craft Path, pointing at the "fun, professional" list on the front of the tent.

Step 6: Recap and hand it to the judge

Close

"So just to recap, we want to have people post on our app about them in front of our stores during National Selfie Day, to build off of buzz marketing and get more views surrounding National Selfie Day, and have them post images specifically since they spread fast. And we are prioritizing having people post on our platforms to protect our corporate image. Now, I know that was a lot, but the marketing team truly worked very hard on this. But that being said, we are more than open to feedback on how to make this better and to know what you think. Did you have any questions for me regarding this?"

What's happening: one breath that hits every PI, then a handoff. Now the judge asks questions.
The whole pattern: intro promises a plan → PIs 1 and 2 explain what we considered → PI 3 reveals the plan → PIs 4 and 5 defend it → recap → questions. The scenario changes every time. This pattern doesn't.
Part 3 · Your Turn

Practice roleplay: Fresh Grounds Coffee

Same steps, new scenario. Set a 10-minute timer for prep and a 7-minute timer for the roleplay, and do it out loud with someone playing the judge.

Event situation: You are a marketing coordinator at Fresh Grounds Coffee, a regional coffee chain expanding onto college campuses. You've been called into a meeting with the Vice President of Marketing (the judge). Fresh Grounds has seen a 30% drop in engagement from the 18–24 demographic over the last year. Develop a strategy to re-engage college students and increase foot traffic at campus locations.

The PIs

PI 1
Explain the concept of market segmentation.
PI 2
Describe the role of social media in marketing.
PI 3
Identify strategies for customer retention.
PI 4
Explain how technology can enhance the customer experience.

Prep room: fill it in

Work through the same steps as the Craft Path walkthrough. Your answers save on this device, so you can come back to them.

💻 Technology🤖 AI📱 Social media🎯 Events🤝 Partnerships♻️ Repurpose
Write it messy first, then tighten it.
PI 1 · Market segmentationPI 2 · Social mediaPI 3 · Customer retentionPI 4 · Technology

Your four tents

For each tent: what it is, why it's good, what we're doing with it. Then note what you'd draw on the judge's side.

Repeat the problem in their words, say the team worked hard on a plan, and end with a question that leads into PI 1.

Now do it out loud, timed, with someone playing the judge. Then compare:

See one way to do it (only after you've tried it)

Solution: use AI to find the campus moments with the most foot traffic (finals week, morning commute). Run geo-targeted Instagram posts featuring real students at Fresh Grounds. Anyone who posts their study spot at Fresh Grounds is entered to win a semester of free coffee. Campus ambassadors host study events in the store.

Reveal PI: PI 2, social media, because the plan is posts. PI 1 sets up who we're targeting. PIs 3 and 4 defend the plan: the free-coffee entry keeps people coming back, and the AI targeting is the technology.

Intro: "Thank you for meeting with me. I saw your note about the drop in 18–24 engagement, and the team has been working hard on a plan to bring students back. Before I share it, I want to walk you through what we had to consider, and the first thing was: who exactly are we trying to reach?"

Part 4 · Level Up (after your first roleplay)

Level up

Once you've done a full roleplay, these will make yours stronger.

Say "as you know"

When you name a PI, lead with "as you know." It boosts the judge's confidence and makes you sound like you're in a real meeting, not reciting a definition.

Raise the objection before the judge does

"Now, I realize we may have some concerns about..." turns a weakness into a PI you get credit for. Use it on whichever PI is about risk, monitoring, or cost.

Prepare for the questions

On your side of the last tent, write the two questions you'd least want to be asked, usually "how much does this cost?" and "what if it doesn't work?", with a one-line answer under each. The questions are scored, and most people prepare nothing.

If you blank

Say "Let me come back to that in a second. The more important piece here is..." and move to your next tent. Judges score recovery much better than silence.

Two drills to do every day

The 1-minute speech drill. Pick any random word ("umbrella," "momentum," "trust"). Take 10 seconds to think, then talk about it for 60 seconds straight without stopping. This trains thinking on your feet, which is exactly what the judge's questions demand.
The segue drill. Pick two random concepts and connect them in one sentence. "Corporate branding → selfies": "A brand is what our customers post about us, which is exactly why a selfie campaign is a branding play." Do it until it's automatic.

Other events

In finance, hospitality, or HR roleplays, your solution buckets are process, training, and cost structure. The reveal PI is whichever one is about the thing your plan changes.

The whole system
  1. Fold your tents and write a PI on each.
  2. Read the situation and pick a solution.
  3. Pick the PI where the solution fits best.
  4. Each tent: what it is, why it's good, what we're doing with it. Draw the judge's side.
  5. Handshake, intro that promises a plan, segue into PI 1.
  6. Set up → reveal → defend → recap → questions.
